source.title: An Embarrassingly Simple Defense Against LLM Abliteration Attacks
source.authors: H. Shairah; Hasan Abed Al Kader Hammoud; Bernard Ghanem; G. Turkiyyah

record.tranche_reason: The study applies the difference-in-means refusal-direction method and projection-based weight ablation to instruction-tuned models, then measures refusal and utility. It compares base models with extended-refusal fine-tuned variants.
record.gate_note: The main ablation results are in Table 1. Figure 2 sweeps candidate layer-position directions, but those results are used to select the direction and are not separately extracted. Table 2 reports other jailbreak benchmarks, not attacks shown to suppress the refusal direction, so those results are not rows for these versions. Section 4.4 also reports centroid-distance measurements, recorded under fits_no_version because they do not measure refusal or the number or geometry of refusal directions directly.
record.test_reason: The study applies the original difference-in-means direction selection and the projection weight edit to Llama-2-7B-Chat and Qwen2.5-1.5B/3B-Instruct. It measures refusal (CatQA, LLM judge) and utility (coherence, MMLU, perplexity) before and after. It repeats this on its own extended-refusal fine-tuned variants and on component-only variants. These results bear on V1, V2 and V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly right. The authors conclude that extended-refusal fine-tuning makes models robust to abliteration: refusal stays above 90% versus 13–21% for standard models, a drop of at most ~9 points versus 70–80. They attribute this to dispersing the refusal signal across multiple latent dimensions, which they do not test directly. They also report better robustness to other jailbreaks and to benign fine-tuning. They acknowledge greater utility and coherence loss when ER models are abliterated, and say pre-ablation costs are minimal.
record.recipe_differences: The study follows the described difference-in-means candidate-direction selection and projection-based output-weight edit. It tests base instruction-tuned models and variants fine-tuned on its extended-refusal dataset; direction selection also filters for coherence above 70%.
record.method_sensitivity: The selected direction is chosen from layer-position candidates to maximize refusal degradation subject to coherence above 70%. The study reports different utility and refusal outcomes across candidate directions in Figure 2, but does not extract those selection-sweep values as rows.

fits_no_version.finding: After ablation, harmful–benign centroid distance in PCA of final hidden states falls 28.7–33.9 points in standard models but only 7.7–13.7 in ER models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Extended-refusal fine-tuning preserves harmful-versus-benign representation separation after abliteration.

record.problems: The study reports no uncertainty estimates. Refusal is evaluated using automated judges, although Appendix A compares two judges. The tested models are up to 7B parameters. The authors report that extended-refusal variants can lose coherence and other utility after ablation, with a marked perplexity increase for Qwen2.5-1.5B-Extended.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted because of the 60-row limit. Figure 2's candidate-direction sweep is not separately extracted because the paper uses it to select a direction. Table 2's non-directional jailbreak benchmarks and the benign-fine-tuning results are not rows for the listed claim versions.

untested.parts: Adding the direction to induce refusal on harmless prompts is not tested.
Only three released instruct models up to 7B are tested; larger or other released models are not.
Untested. Table 2 jailbreaks are not linked to the direction, and the defense is extended-refusal SFT, not training against ablation.
Authors assert refusal is dispersed across multiple dimensions but ablate only one direction at a time; no multi-direction or cone analysis.
Not tested; the centroid-distance analysis uses harmful vs benign prompts and does not separate harm judgment from refusal.
When refusal is trained (pre- vs post-training timing) is not varied; only the form of refusal responses is varied.

missing.what: Sweep over every candidate layer×position direction for ER models. No direction lowers refusal without also lowering MMLU and raising perplexity; Qwen-1.5B-ER positions −2 and −5 give no coherent model. This bears on whether any single removable direction exists after ER training. Values must be read from the figures.

record.verdict_notes: Base models' refusal is 100 for Llama and 93.1/93.8 for Qwen. Direction selection maximizes refusal drop subject to coherence ≥70%, so ER-model results reflect the best single direction under that filter. Refusal is judged by Qwen-2.5-14B with a general safe/unsafe prompt, so incoherent output counts as 'safe'. Some ER post-ablation 'refusal' may therefore be degeneration (Appendix C), which weakens the reading that refusal is preserved. No uncertainty is reported. Dataset counts differ between Sections 3.2 (4,289/5,711) and 4.1 (4,268/5,732).

versions.untested_parts: The study does not add the direction to induce refusals on harmless requests. It tests removal and utility effects.
The weight edit is tested on the study's selected instruction-tuned models; broader released-model coverage is not tested.
It tests resistance to the paper's abliteration procedure after extended-refusal fine-tuning. It does not establish that other attacks work by suppressing this direction.
The study does not compare affine, cone, or dominant-plus-other-directions descriptions.
No separate harmfulness-judgment and refusal-decision representation is tested.
No cross-language, base-to-instruct, or model-variant transfer of a direction is tested.
The study compares standard and extended-refusal training and individual refusal components, but does not vary when refusal training occurs.

relation.reason: The study's own before/after abliteration results on standard and ER-trained models bear directly on V1, V2 and V7.

tranche.reason: Uses the original's difference-in-means candidates, refusal-drop selection and output-matrix projection edit, and measures refusal before and after on new models. The judge and prompt set (CatQA, Qwen-2.5-14B) differ, but the method and the construct are the same.

source_check.notes: The 'refusal score' is the % of CatQA responses the Qwen-2.5-14B judge labels SAFE, so incoherent post-ablation output from ER models (Appendix C, coherence 89.1-98.7%) can count as refusal. Appendix A says the two judges differ by at most 4 points, but 96.7 vs 89.3 is 7.4. Dataset counts also differ between sections (4,289/5,711 in Sec 3.2 vs 4,268/5,732 in Sec 4.1).

statements.correction: r01/r09/r17 use only the Qwen-2.5-14B safe/unsafe judge on CatQA (550 harmful questions). The Llama-Guard-3-8B comparison (Table 4) covers only the ER-abliterated variants.
statements.problem: Minor: 'two judges compared' could be read as covering the cited standard-model drops. Llama-Guard-3-8B was run only on the three ER-abliterated models.

statements.correction: The Qwen-2.5-14B judge classifies responses as safe/unsafe (Fig. 9). The refusal score is the % judged safe on CatQA (550 harmful questions), so 20.7 means about 79% unsafe. The system prompt is not stated. The direction is chosen to maximise refusal drop with coherence above 70%.
statements.problem: The 100.0->20.7 is right, but the stated differences call the judge a 'refusal judge' and leave out the prompt set. The judge labels responses SAFE/UNSAFE, which matters when comparing with ASR or unsafe rates.
Minor: the text cites r25-r27, but the cited-rows list has only r25.

statements.correction: ER fine-tuning is standard SFT (3 epochs, lr 1e-6, 10k examples) on refusals written to diffuse the refusal signal. It was designed to defeat abliteration (title; Sec 3.2), not as an ordinary alignment choice.
statements.problem: The statement counts extended refusals as an 'ordinary training choice'. The paper builds and presents ER fine-tuning explicitly as a defense against abliteration, though its objective is plain SFT with no ablation in the loop.
